title: Morning puja
hook: the whole thing in four minutes

segments.voice: Yesterday, naivedya, the sweet that goes to the shrine first. Your line was shared. Did you give away a first piece of something? Day one hundred and seventeen.

Look at this week. It started with five objects and a corner that's yours. Then one flame, the lamp. A flower, fresh, daily. A bell that helps you arrive. Water: washed, given, received. And a sweet that goes to the shrine first and comes back to be shared. Six days, six pieces, laid out on the table like parts of a watch. Today we put the watch together. People sometimes imagine puja as a long, complicated ceremony that only a priest can run. At a temple on a festival day, it can be. At home, on a Tuesday, before work, it can be four minutes.
screen: `A WEEK OF PIECES.` → `NOT JUST FOR PRIESTS.` → `TODAY: PUT IT TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Puja, the word from day eight, means honoring, worship, and the old line from that day still holds: attention is an offering. Full temple worship can have sixteen services, the whole welcome of a royal guest. Many homes use a short form, and old manuals even name a five-part version: fragrance, flower, incense, lamp and food. Your week covers almost all of it. So here's one simple morning shape. Families do it in different orders, and none is the only right one. First, begin clean: wash, or sip a little water. Then ring the bell, and let it bring you here. Light the lamp. Offer a flower, and a few drops of water. Set down something sweet. Then comes the heart of it: a few moments of mantra, the one from last week that fits you, Om or Om namah shivaya or the Gayatri, or simply the name you honor, said quietly. Then pranam, the bow from day five: hands together, head down. And last, take a little of the sweet back as prasad, and share the rest later. That's it. Bell, lamp, flower, water, food, name, bow. Some mornings you'll do all of it. Some mornings you'll just light the lamp and bow. Many grandmothers would tell you that counts too. The point was never the full list. The point is that before the day grabs you, something else gets the first four minutes.
screen: `PUJA — ATTENTION IS AN OFFERING.` · `A FIVE-PART FORM FOR HOME.` · `BELL, LAMP, FLOWER, WATER, FOOD.` · `A NAME, A BOW, THE SWEET RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Let's do it together, however small your corner is, even if it's only in your mind. Ring the bell, or tap a glass, and listen until it fades. Light the lamp, or picture it. Set down a flower or a leaf. A few drops of water. A small piece of something sweet. Now, quietly, say your mantra or a name you honor, if you'd like, a few times. Hands together. Bow. The rest of the time is yours to sit in front of it. The bell holds the time.
Morning puja. The home shrine, put together: bell, lamp, flower, water, food, a name and a bow, before the day begins. Today's word.

Your line: four minutes. Tomorrow morning, before your phone, give four minutes to your corner, any version of it. That's the week. Tomorrow we move to the other end of the day. Day one hundred and seventeen.

howItsDone: Many Hindu households do a short daily puja at the home shrine in the morning: ringing a bell, lighting a lamp, offering flowers, water and food, saying a mantra or a deity's name, bowing, and sharing the offered food as prasad.

original.note: Sanskrit pūjā: honoring, worship. Your word from day eight.

trapdoor: what you thought: a long ritual only priests can run.
what it means: a few minutes at the home shrine: bell, lamp, flower, water, food, a name and a bow, before the day begins.
what a scholar hears: puja manuals describe sixteen upacharas (shodashopachara) for full worship and a five-part panchopachara (gandha, pushpa, dhupa, dipa, naivedya) for shorter worship.
